subproblem.title: The radial retraction onto a closed ball is 1-Lipschitz
subproblem.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ and ρ ∈ ℝ with ρ > 0, and give ℝ^P = Euclid P the Euclidean norm. Then there is a map r : ℝ^P → ℝ^P such that (1) r is 1-Lipschitz, i.e. ‖r(x) − r(y)‖ ≤ ‖x − y‖ for all x, y (LipschitzWith 1 r); (2) ‖r(y)‖ ≤ ρ for every y ∈ ℝ^P; (3) r(y) = y for every y with ‖y‖ ≤ ρ. (For example the nearest-point retraction r(y) = y for ‖y‖ ≤ ρ and r(y) = (ρ/‖y‖)·y otherwise.)
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (ρ : ℝ), 0 < ρ → ∃ r : Euclid P → Euclid P, LipschitzWith 1 r ∧ (∀ y, ‖r y‖ ≤ ρ) ∧ ∀ y, ‖y‖ ≤ ρ → r y = y
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Step 2 of the selected node's supplied proof (F1 of the cone-filling proof). There the radial retraction r_ρ onto B̄ := closedBall(0, ρ) is the nearest-point projection onto a closed convex set, and the variational-inequality argument below is the one given there, with every case written out.

Proof. Fix P and ρ > 0, and write B̄ := {z ∈ ℝ^P : ‖z‖ ≤ ρ}.
1. (Definition.) For y ∈ ℝ^P put r(y) := y if ‖y‖ ≤ ρ and r(y) := (ρ/‖y‖)·y if ‖y‖ > ρ. Property (3) holds by definition.
2. (Property (2).) If ‖y‖ ≤ ρ, then ‖r(y)‖ = ‖y‖ ≤ ρ. If ‖y‖ > ρ, then ‖y‖ > 0 and ρ/‖y‖ > 0, so ‖r(y)‖ = (ρ/‖y‖)·‖y‖ = ρ. In particular r(y) ∈ B̄ for every y.
3. (Variational inequality.) Claim: for every x ∈ ℝ^P and every z ∈ B̄, with p := r(x), ⟨x − p, z − p⟩ ≤ 0.
 - Case ‖x‖ ≤ ρ: p = x, so x − p = 0 and the inner product is 0.
 - Case ‖x‖ > ρ: put c := 1 − ρ/‖x‖ > 0. Then p = (ρ/‖x‖)·x and x − p = c·x.
   Moreover ⟨x, p⟩ = (ρ/‖x‖)·‖x‖² = ρ‖x‖.
   By Cauchy–Schwarz (real_inner_le_norm) and ‖z‖ ≤ ρ, ⟨x, z⟩ ≤ ‖x‖‖z‖ ≤ ρ‖x‖.
   Hence ⟨x − p, z − p⟩ = c·(⟨x, z⟩ − ⟨x, p⟩) ≤ c·(ρ‖x‖ − ρ‖x‖) = 0.
4. (1-Lipschitz.) Let x, y ∈ ℝ^P, p := r(x) and q := r(y). By step 2, p, q ∈ B̄.
   Step 3 for x and z := q gives ⟨x − p, q − p⟩ ≤ 0. Step 3 for y and z := p gives ⟨y − q, p − q⟩ ≤ 0.
   Add the two inequalities and use (x − p) − (y − q) = (x − y) − (p − q):
   0 ≥ ⟨x − p, q − p⟩ − ⟨y − q, q − p⟩ = ⟨(x − y) − (p − q), q − p⟩ = ‖p − q‖² − ⟨x − y, p − q⟩.
   Hence ‖p − q‖² ≤ ⟨x − y, p − q⟩ ≤ ‖x − y‖·‖p − q‖ by Cauchy–Schwarz.
   If p = q, then ‖p − q‖ = 0 ≤ ‖x − y‖. Otherwise divide by ‖p − q‖ > 0 to get ‖p − q‖ ≤ ‖x − y‖.
   Thus dist(r(x), r(y)) ≤ 1·dist(x, y) for all x, y, i.e. r is 1-Lipschitz (LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul with constant 1).
Steps 1–4 give r with (1), (2) and (3). ∎
proof_key_steps: Define r(y) = y on the closed ball and r(y) = (ρ/‖y‖)·y outside it; then ‖r(y)‖ ≤ ρ and r fixes the ball.
Variational inequality ⟨x − r(x), z − r(x)⟩ ≤ 0 for every z in the ball: x − r(x) is a nonnegative multiple of x, and ⟨x, z⟩ ≤ ρ‖x‖ = ⟨x, r(x)⟩.
Adding the inequalities for (x, z = r(y)) and (y, z = r(x)) gives ‖r(x) − r(y)‖² ≤ ⟨x − y, r(x) − r(y)⟩ ≤ ‖x − y‖‖r(x) − r(y)‖, so r is 1-Lipschitz.

subproblem.title: Cone Jacobian: Gram-determinant scaling J(a, tw) = t^k J(a, w) and the bound J(a, w) ≤ ‖a‖ J(w)
subproblem.statement: Let P, k ∈ ℕ, a ∈ ℝ^P (Euclid P) and w = (w_0, …, w_{k−1}) with every w_i ∈ ℝ^P. For a finite family v = (v_0, …, v_m) of vectors of ℝ^P let Γ(v) := det[⟨v_i, v_j⟩]_{i,j}, i.e. Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun i j => inner ℝ (v i) (v j)) (Γ of the empty family is 1), and let J(v) := √Γ(v), with Real.sqrt, which is 0 on negative numbers. Write (a, w) := Fin.cons a w = (a, w_0, …, w_{k−1}) (a family indexed by Fin (k+1)) and, for t ∈ ℝ, t·w := (t w_0, …, t w_{k−1}). Then: (i) J(a, t·w) = t^k·J(a, w) for every t ≥ 0; (ii) J(a, w) ≤ ‖a‖·J(w).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P k : ℕ) (a : Euclid P) (w : Fin k → Euclid P), (∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → Real.sqrt (Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun i j : Fin (k + 1) => inner ℝ ((Fin.cons a (t • w) : Fin (k + 1) → Euclid P) i) ((Fin.cons a (t • w) : Fin (k + 1) → Euclid P) j))) = t ^ k * Real.sqrt (Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun i j : Fin (k + 1) => inner ℝ ((Fin.cons a w : Fin (k + 1) → Euclid P) i) ((Fin.cons a w : Fin (k + 1) → Euclid P) j)))) ∧ Real.sqrt (Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun i j : Fin (k + 1) => inner ℝ ((Fin.cons a w : Fin (k + 1) → Euclid P) i) ((Fin.cons a w : Fin (k + 1) → Euclid P) j))) ≤ ‖a‖ * Real.sqrt (Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun i j : Fin k => inner ℝ (w i) (w j)))
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Step 6 of the selected node's supplied proof (A4, the cone Jacobian, of the cone-filling proof). It is the Jacobian computation behind Simon 6.2.30 and 6.3.10 for h(t, x) = tx.
Notation as in the statement. For a family v indexed by Fin m, M(v) denotes the m×m Gram matrix (⟨v_i, v_j⟩)_{i,j}, so Γ(v) = det M(v). Index Fin (k+1) by 0, 1, …, k, so that (a, w)_0 = a and (a, w)_{i+1} = w_i (Fin.cons_zero, Fin.cons_succ).

Part (i).
1. Let d ∈ ℝ^{k+1} have d_0 := 1 and d_{i+1} := t (d = Fin.cons 1 (fun _ => t)), and let D := diag(d).
   The family (a, t·w) equals (d_i·v_i)_i with v := (a, w): its 0-th member is a = 1·a, and its (i+1)-st is t·w_i (Fin.cons_succ, Pi.smul_apply).
2. By bilinearity, ⟨d_i v_i, d_j v_j⟩ = d_i d_j ⟨v_i, v_j⟩. Hence M(a, t·w) = D·M(a, w)·D (entrywise, (D M D)_{ij} = d_i M_{ij} d_j).
3. Hence Γ(a, t·w) = det D · Γ(a, w) · det D = (∏_i d_i)²·Γ(a, w) = (t^k)²·Γ(a, w).
   This uses Matrix.det_mul and Matrix.det_diagonal, and ∏_i d_i = 1·t^k (Fin.prod_univ_succ, product of the constant t over Fin k).
4. Since (t^k)² ≥ 0, Real.sqrt_mul gives √((t^k)²·Γ(a, w)) = √((t^k)²)·√Γ(a, w); that lemma needs only the first factor nonnegative, whatever the sign of Γ(a, w).
   Moreover √((t^k)²) = t^k because t^k ≥ 0 for t ≥ 0 (Real.sqrt_sq). Thus J(a, t·w) = t^k·J(a, w).

Part (ii).
5. Let W := span{w_0, …, w_{k−1}} ⊆ ℝ^P. W is finite-dimensional, so the orthogonal projection π onto W exists (Submodule.starProjection; finite-dimensional subspaces have HasOrthogonalProjection). Put a' := a − π(a).
   Then a' ∈ W^⊥ (Submodule.sub_starProjection_mem_orthogonal), so ⟨a', w_i⟩ = ⟨w_i, a'⟩ = 0 for every i.
   Since π(a) ∈ W, there are c_0, …, c_{k−1} ∈ ℝ with π(a) = Σ_i c_i w_i (Submodule.mem_span_range_iff_exists_fun).
   Finally ⟨a', π(a)⟩ = 0, so by Pythagoras (norm_add_sq_eq_norm_sq_add_norm_sq_of_inner_eq_zero) ‖a‖² = ‖a' + π(a)‖² = ‖a'‖² + ‖π(a)‖² ≥ ‖a'‖². Hence ‖a'‖ ≤ ‖a‖.
6. (Column operation.) Let v := (a, w) and v' := (a', w), and let E be the (k+1)×(k+1) matrix with
   E_{0,0} = 1, E_{i+1,0} = −c_i, E_{0,j+1} = 0 and E_{i+1,j+1} = δ_{ij}.
   Then v'_j = Σ_l E_{l,j} v_l for every j: for j = 0 the right side is a − Σ_i c_i w_i = a', and for j = i+1 it is w_i.
   By bilinearity ⟨v'_i, v'_j⟩ = Σ_{l,m} E_{l,i}⟨v_l, v_m⟩E_{m,j}, i.e. M(v') = Eᵀ·M(v)·E.
   E is lower triangular with every diagonal entry 1, so det E = 1 (Matrix.det_of_isLowerTriangular), and det Eᵀ = det E = 1 (Matrix.det_transpose).
   By Matrix.det_mul, Γ(a', w) = Γ(a, w).
   (Equivalently: Γ is unchanged when multiples of the other vectors are subtracted from v_0, because this subtracts the same multiples of other rows and of other columns of M(v).)
7. (Block structure.) By step 5, the first row of M(v') is (‖a'‖², ⟨a', w_0⟩, …, ⟨a', w_{k−1}⟩) = (‖a'‖², 0, …, 0).
   Deleting row 0 and column 0 of M(v') leaves (⟨w_i, w_j⟩)_{i,j} = M(w).
   Expanding det M(v') along row 0 (Matrix.det_succ_row_zero), only the j = 0 term survives: Γ(a', w) = ‖a'‖²·Γ(w).
8. Steps 6 and 7 give Γ(a, w) = ‖a'‖²·Γ(w).
   As in step 4 (Real.sqrt_mul with ‖a'‖² ≥ 0, and Real.sqrt_sq with ‖a'‖ ≥ 0), J(a, w) = √(‖a'‖²·Γ(w)) = ‖a'‖·J(w).
   Since 0 ≤ ‖a'‖ ≤ ‖a‖ (step 5) and J(w) ≥ 0, J(a, w) ≤ ‖a‖·J(w).

Remarks.
 - The parent text first disposes of linearly dependent w, where both Gram determinants vanish. Steps 5–8 never use independence of w: the coefficients c_i exist in every case. So no case distinction is needed, and the bound holds for all w.
 - For k = 0, W = {0}, π(a) = 0, a' = a and E = (1). M(w) is the empty matrix with determinant 1, and step 8 reads √(‖a‖²) = ‖a‖ ≤ ‖a‖·1.
Parts (i) and (ii) are proved. ∎
proof_key_steps: Gram(a, t·w) = D·Gram(a, w)·D with D = diag(1, t, …, t), so Γ(a, t·w) = t^{2k}Γ(a, w) and J(a, t·w) = t^k J(a, w) for t ≥ 0.
With a′ := a − π_W a (W = span w, π_W a = Σ c_i w_i), the unipotent column operation E gives Gram(a′, w) = Eᵀ·Gram(a, w)·E, hence Γ(a, w) = Γ(a′, w).
a′ ⊥ W makes the first row of Gram(a′, w) equal to (‖a′‖², 0, …, 0); Laplace expansion gives Γ(a′, w) = ‖a′‖²Γ(w).
J(a, w) = ‖a′‖·J(w) ≤ ‖a‖·J(w) by Pythagoras; no independence of w is needed.

Orthogonal projection and the explicit unipotent matrix prove the determinant factorization without assuming independence of w, including k = 0. The square-root steps require only the stated nonnegative first factors. No circularity or missing hypothesis remains.

   Since ‖z‖² = Σ_{i≤k} z_i², we have |s(z)| ≤ ‖z‖ and ‖τ(z)‖ ≤ ‖z‖. By linearity, |s(z) − s(z')| ≤ ‖z − z'‖ and ‖τ(z) − τ(z')‖ ≤ ‖z − z'‖.
   Moreover s(ι(t, u)) = t and τ(ι(t, u)) = u (WithLp.ofLp_toLp, Fin.cons_zero, Fin.tail_cons, WithLp.toLp_ofLp).
   On basis vectors: s(e_0) = 1, τ(e_0) = 0, s(e_{b+1}) = 0 and τ(e_{b+1}) = e'_b. These are the coordinates of EuclideanSpace.single (Pi.single_apply, Fin.succ_ne_zero, Fin.succ_inj).
2. (Retraction.) Apply the sibling lemma ball_retraction to P and ρ > 0. It gives r : ℝ^P → ℝ^P that is 1-Lipschitz, with ‖r(y)‖ ≤ ρ for all y and r(y) = y whenever ‖y‖ ≤ ρ.
   Let L ≥ 0 be a Lipschitz constant of F, and put F̂ := r ∘ F. Then F̂ is L-Lipschitz (LipschitzWith.comp; constant 1·L), ‖F̂(u)‖ ≤ ρ for every u, and F̂(u) = F(u) whenever ‖F(u)‖ ≤ ρ.
3. (Clamp.) Let σ(t) := min(max(t, 0), 1). σ is 1-Lipschitz (LipschitzWith.max_const, LipschitzWith.min_const), 0 ≤ σ(t) ≤ 1, and σ(t) = t for t ∈ [0, 1].
4. (Definition.) G(z) := σ(s(z))·F̂(τ(z)).
5. (G is Lipschitz.) For z, z' ∈ ℝ^{k+1},
   G(z) − G(z') = (σ(s z) − σ(s z'))·F̂(τ z) + σ(s z')·(F̂(τ z) − F̂(τ z')).
   By steps 1–3:
   ‖G(z) − G(z')‖ ≤ |σ(s z) − σ(s z')|·‖F̂(τ z)‖ + |σ(s z')|·‖F̂(τ z) − F̂(τ z')‖ ≤ |s z − s z'|·ρ + 1·L·‖τ z − τ z'‖ ≤ (ρ + L)·‖z − z'‖.
   So G is K-Lipschitz with K := ρ.toNNReal + L (LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul).
6. (Value on the cylinder.) Fix u ∈ A and t ∈ (0, 1), and put z₀ := ι(t, u). Then s(z₀) = t and σ(t) = t. Also τ(z₀) = u and ‖F(u)‖ < ρ, so F̂(u) = F(u). Hence G(z₀) = t·F(u).
7. (Local form.) O := F⁻¹(ball(0, ρ)) is open because F is continuous, and u ∈ O.
   N := s⁻¹((0, 1)) ∩ τ⁻¹(O) is open because s and τ are continuous, and z₀ ∈ N since s(z₀) = t ∈ (0, 1) and τ(z₀) = u ∈ O.
   For z ∈ N, σ(s z) = s z because s z ∈ (0, 1). Also ‖F(τ z)‖ < ρ, so F̂(τ z) = r(F(τ z)) = F(τ z).
   Hence G = H on N, where H(z) := s(z)·F(τ(z)).
   N is a neighbourhood of z₀ (IsOpen.mem_nhds), so G and H agree eventually near z₀ and DG(z₀) = DH(z₀) (Filter.EventuallyEq.fderiv_eq).
8. (Derivative of H.) s is a continuous linear map, so HasFDerivAt s s z₀ (ContinuousLinearMap.hasFDerivAt).
   τ is a continuous linear map with τ(z₀) = u, and F is differentiable at u because u ∈ A. By the chain rule (HasFDerivAt.comp), F ∘ τ has derivative DF(u) ∘ τ at z₀.
   By the product rule for a scalar function times a vector function (HasFDerivAt.smul), H has at z₀ the derivative
   DH(z₀)h = s(z₀)·DF(u)(τ h) + s(h)·F(τ z₀) = t·DF(u)(τ h) + s(h)·F(u) for every h (HasFDerivAt.fderiv).
9. (Evaluation.) By steps 1, 7 and 8:
   DG(z₀)e_0 = t·DF(u)(0) + 1·F(u) = F(u);
   DG(z₀)e_{b+1} = t·DF(u)(e'_b) + 0·F(u) = t·DF(u)e'_b for b < k.
   The family Fin.cons (F u) (t·∂F(u)) takes the value F(u) at 0 and t·DF(u)e'_b at b+1 (Fin.cons_zero, Fin.cons_succ, Pi.smul_apply).
   So the two functions Fin (k+1) → ℝ^P agree at every index (Fin.cases), and ∂G(z₀) = Fin.cons (F u) (t·∂F(u)) by funext.
Steps 5, 6 and 9 prove the claim. ∎

Source: Steps 3(a), 3(c), 5 and 8(a)–(c) of the selected node's supplied proof (F3–F4 of the cone-filling proof; Simon Ch. 6, 2.30 and 3.10, book/chapter-06.txt lines 528–551 and 857–865), specialized to one piece.
CF(a), CF(b), CF(c) denote parts (a), (b), (c) of the sibling cylinder_fubini, i.e. the reused accepted lemma cmcdt_lpi_cyl_fubini applied with n := k and this Borel set A. Its cylinder is exactly Cyl(A), and its ι(t, u) is WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.cons t (WithLp.ofLp u)).

Proof.
1. (τ and ι.) τ is linear in finitely many coordinates, hence continuous and Borel measurable. For t ∈ ℝ and u ∈ ℝ^k, τ(ι(t, u)) = u and (WithLp.ofLp ι(t, u)) 0 = t (WithLp.ofLp_toLp, Fin.tail_cons, Fin.cons_zero, WithLp.toLp_ofLp).
2. (Part (a).) g and τ are measurable, so g ∘ τ is measurable (Measurable.comp). The coercion ℤ → ℝ is measurable (ℤ has the discrete σ-algebra).
   Hence z ↦ (g(τ z) : ℝ) is measurable, and so is the [0, ∞]-valued z ↦ ‖(g(τ z) : ℝ)‖ₑ.
3. (Part (b).) By CF(b) with f(z) := ‖(g(τ z) : ℝ)‖ₑ and step 1,
   ∫⁻_{Cyl(A)} ‖g(τ z)‖ₑ dz = ∫⁻_{u∈A} ∫⁻_{t∈(0,1)} ‖g(u)‖ₑ dt du = ∫⁻_{u∈A} ‖g(u)‖ₑ·λ((0,1)) du = ∫⁻_A ‖g(u)‖ₑ du.
   Here the inner integrand is constant in t (setLIntegral_const) and λ((0,1)) = ofReal(1 − 0) = 1 (Real.volume_Ioo).
   The last integral is finite because (g : ℝ) is integrable on A.
   z ↦ (g(τ z) : ℝ) is measurable (step 2), so it is a.e.-strongly measurable for λ restricted to Cyl(A). With the finite integral above, it is integrable on Cyl(A).
4. (Bounds.) ω is continuous with compact support, so there is M with ‖ω(y)‖ ≤ M for all y ∈ ℝ^P (HasCompactSupport.exists_bound_of_continuous; operator norm of the continuous alternating map ω(y)). Necessarily M ≥ 0.
   G is K-Lipschitz for some K ≥ 0, so ‖DG(z)‖ ≤ K for every z (norm_fderiv_le_of_lipschitz).
   Hence ‖DG(z)e_a‖ ≤ ‖DG(z)‖·‖e_a‖ = ‖DG(z)‖ ≤ K for every z and every index a, as ‖e_a‖ = 1.
5. (Measurability of the integrand.) Put Φ(z) := (g(τ z) : ℝ)·ω(G z)(∂G(z)).
   z ↦ DG(z) is Borel measurable (measurable_fderiv), so each z ↦ DG(z)e_a is measurable (measurable_fderiv_apply_const), and z ↦ ∂G(z) ∈ (ℝ^P)^{k+1} is measurable (measurable_pi_iff).
   G is continuous, so z ↦ (G(z), ∂G(z)) ∈ ℝ^P × (ℝ^P)^{k+1} is measurable (Measurable.prodMk).
   The map Ψ(y, v) := ω(y)(v) on ℝ^P × (ℝ^P)^{k+1} is continuous: ω is continuous, and evaluation of continuous alternating maps is jointly continuous (ContinuousAlternatingMap.instContinuousEval, Continuous.eval).
   So Ψ is Borel measurable, and z ↦ ω(G z)(∂G(z)) = Ψ(G z, ∂G z) is measurable. With step 2, Φ is measurable.
6. (Integrability of Φ.) For every z, |ω(G z)(∂G(z))| ≤ ‖ω(G z)‖·∏_{a=0}^{k} ‖DG(z)e_a‖ ≤ M·K^{k+1} (ContinuousAlternatingMap.le_opNorm and step 4).
   So |Φ(z)| ≤ M K^{k+1}·|g(τ z)|. The right-hand side is integrable on Cyl(A) by part (b) (Integrable.const_mul), and Φ is measurable (step 5).
   Hence Φ is integrable on Cyl(A) (Integrable.mono').
7. (Fubini.) By CF(c) applied to Φ, which is integrable on Cyl(A) by step 6:
   ∫_{Cyl(A)} Φ = ∫_{u∈A} ∫_{t∈(0,1)} Φ(ι(t, u)) dt du.
8. (Integrand on the cylinder; multilinearity.) Fix u ∈ A and t ∈ (0, 1). By step 1 and the hypotheses, g(τ(ι(t, u))) = g(u), G(ι(t, u)) = t·F(u) and ∂G(ι(t, u)) = Fin.cons (F u) (t·∂F(u)).
   Let c := Fin.cons 1 (fun _ => t) ∈ ℝ^{k+1} and v := Fin.cons (F u) (∂F(u)). Then Fin.cons (F u) (t·∂F(u)) = (c_a·v_a)_a: at a = 0 both sides are 1·F(u), and at a = b+1 both are t·DF(u)e'_b.
   ω(y) is multilinear, so ω(y)((c_a v_a)_a) = (∏_a c_a)·ω(y)(v) = t^k·ω(y)(v) (ContinuousAlternatingMap.map_smul_univ; ∏_a c_a = 1·t^k by Fin.prod_univ_succ and Finset.prod_const).
   Hence Φ(ι(t, u)) = g(u)·(t^k·ω(t·F(u))(Fin.cons (F u) (∂F(u)))).
9. (Inner integral.) Fix u ∈ A. By step 8 the two integrands below agree on (0, 1) (setIntegral_congr_fun with measurableSet_Ioo), and g(u) is a constant factor (integral_const_mul):
   ∫_{t∈(0,1)} Φ(ι(t, u)) dt = ∫_{(0,1)} g(u)·(t^k ω(tF(u))(Fin.cons (F u) (∂F u))) dt = g(u)·∫_{(0,1)} t^k ω(tF(u))(Fin.cons (F u) (∂F u)) dt.
   Moreover ∫_{(0,1)} h = ∫_{(0,1]} h = ∫_0^1 h for every h: λ has no atoms (integral_Ioc_eq_integral_Ioo), and intervalIntegral.integral_of_le applies with 0 ≤ 1.
10. (Outer integral.) A is measurable, and by step 9 the two functions of u agree on A. By setIntegral_congr_fun,
   ∫_A ∫_{(0,1)} Φ(ι(t, u)) dt du = ∫_A g(u)·(∫_0^1 t^k ω(tF(u))(Fin.cons (F u) (∂F u)) dt) du.
   Together with step 7 this is (c).
Steps 2, 3 and 10 prove (a), (b) and (c). ∎

subproblem.title: One piece of the cone parametrization: ∫⁻_{Cyl(A)} |g(τ)|·JG ≤ ρ ∫⁻_A |g|·JF
subproblem.statement: Let k, P ∈ ℕ, F : ℝ^k → ℝ^P, A ⊆ ℝ^k Borel, g : ℝ^k → ℤ measurable, G : ℝ^{k+1} → ℝ^P and ρ ∈ ℝ. Notation: ι(t, u) := WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.cons t (WithLp.ofLp u)); τ(z) := WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.tail (WithLp.ofLp z)); Cyl(A) := {z ∈ ℝ^{k+1} : (WithLp.ofLp z) 0 ∈ (0, 1), τ(z) ∈ A}; DH(z) := fderiv ℝ H z; e_a := EuclideanSpace.single a 1; ∂H(z) := (DH(z)e_a)_a; and JH(z) := √det[⟨DH(z)e_a, DH(z)e_b⟩]_{a,b} (Real.sqrt). Assume ‖F(u)‖ ≤ ρ for every u ∈ A, and ∂G(ι(t, u)) = Fin.cons (F(u)) (t·∂F(u)) for all u ∈ A and t ∈ (0, 1). Then ∫⁻_{Cyl(A)} ‖(g(τ z) : ℝ)‖ₑ·ofReal(JG(z)) dz ≤ ofReal(ρ)·∫⁻_A ‖(g(u) : ℝ)‖ₑ·ofReal(JF(u)) du. These are lower Lebesgue integrals in [0, ∞]; ‖·‖ₑ is the extended norm, i.e. the absolute value, and ofReal is ENNReal.ofReal.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (k P : ℕ) (F : Euclid k → Euclid P) (A : Set (Euclid k)) (g : Euclid k → ℤ) (G : Euclid (k + 1) → Euclid P) (ρ : ℝ), MeasurableSet A → Measurable g → (∀ u ∈ A, ‖F u‖ ≤ ρ) → (∀ u ∈ A, ∀ t ∈ Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1, (fun a => fderiv ℝ G (WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.cons t (WithLp.ofLp u))) (EuclideanSpace.single a 1)) = (Fin.cons (F u) (t • fun b => fderiv ℝ F u (EuclideanSpace.single b 1)) : Fin (k + 1) → Euclid P)) → ∫⁻ z in {z : Euclid (k + 1) | WithLp.ofLp z 0 ∈ Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1 ∧ (WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.tail (WithLp.ofLp z)) : Euclid k) ∈ A}, ‖(g (WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.tail (WithLp.ofLp z))) : ℝ)‖ₑ * ENNReal.ofReal (Real.sqrt (Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun a b : Fin (k + 1) => inner ℝ (fderiv ℝ G z (EuclideanSpace.single a 1)) (fderiv ℝ G z (EuclideanSpace.single b 1))))) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal ρ * ∫⁻ u in A, ‖(g u : ℝ)‖ₑ * ENNReal.ofReal (Real.sqrt (Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun a b : Fin k => inner ℝ (fderiv ℝ F u (EuclideanSpace.single a 1)) (fderiv ℝ F u (EuclideanSpace.single b 1)))))
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Steps 6 and 7 of the selected node's supplied proof (A4 and F5 of the cone-filling proof), specialized to one piece.
CF(b) denotes part (b) of the sibling cylinder_fubini (cmcdt_lpi_cyl_fubini with n := k and this A; its cylinder is Cyl(A)). GC(i) and GC(ii) denote the two parts of the sibling gram_cone. J(v) := √det[⟨v_i, v_j⟩] as there.

Proof.
1. (Measurability.) Let f(z) := ‖(g(τ z) : ℝ)‖ₑ·ofReal(JG(z)).
   τ is continuous and g is measurable, so z ↦ g(τ z) is measurable, and hence so is z ↦ ‖(g(τ z) : ℝ)‖ₑ.
   For each pair (a, b), z ↦ DG(z)e_a is measurable (measurable_fderiv_apply_const). The inner product is continuous (continuous_inner), so z ↦ ⟨DG(z)e_a, DG(z)e_b⟩ is measurable.
   The determinant of a (k+1)×(k+1) matrix is a finite sum over permutations of signed products of entries (Matrix.det_apply). So z ↦ det[⟨DG(z)e_a, DG(z)e_b⟩] is measurable (Finset.measurable_sum, Finset.measurable_prod).
   Composing with the continuous maps Real.sqrt and ENNReal.ofReal, z ↦ ofReal(JG(z)) is measurable. Hence f is measurable.
2. (Tonelli.) By CF(b), ∫⁻_{Cyl(A)} f = ∫⁻_{u∈A} ∫⁻_{t∈(0,1)} f(ι(t, u)) dt du.
3. (Pointwise bound.) Fix u ∈ A and t ∈ (0, 1). Then τ(ι(t, u)) = u (WithLp.ofLp_toLp, Fin.tail_cons, WithLp.toLp_ofLp).
   By hypothesis DG(ι(t, u))e_a = V_a for every a, where V := Fin.cons (F u) (t·∂F(u)). So the Gram matrix in JG(ι(t, u)) is (⟨V_a, V_b⟩)_{a,b}.
   Apply gram_cone with a := F(u) and w := ∂F(u), noting t ≥ 0:
   JG(ι(t, u)) = J(F u, t·∂F(u)) = t^k·J(F u, ∂F(u)) (GC(i)) ≤ t^k·‖F(u)‖·J(∂F(u)) (GC(ii), multiplied by t^k ≥ 0) ≤ ρ·JF(u).
   The last step uses 0 ≤ t^k ≤ 1 (as 0 < t < 1), 0 ≤ ‖F(u)‖ ≤ ρ, and J(∂F(u)) = JF(u) ≥ 0 (a square root).
   Since ρ ≥ ‖F(u)‖ ≥ 0, ofReal(ρ·JF(u)) = ofReal(ρ)·ofReal(JF(u)) (ENNReal.ofReal_mul).
   ENNReal.ofReal and multiplication in [0, ∞] are monotone, so f(ι(t, u)) ≤ ofReal(ρ)·(‖(g(u) : ℝ)‖ₑ·ofReal(JF(u))) =: c_u.
4. (Inner integral.) For u ∈ A, step 3 and monotonicity of the integral on the measurable set (0, 1) (setLIntegral_mono') give
   ∫⁻_{t∈(0,1)} f(ι(t, u)) dt ≤ ∫⁻_{(0,1)} c_u dt = c_u·λ((0,1)) = c_u (setLIntegral_const, Real.volume_Ioo).
5. (Outer integral.) Step 4 and monotonicity on the measurable set A (setLIntegral_mono') give
   ∫⁻_{u∈A} ∫⁻_{t∈(0,1)} f(ι(t, u)) dt du ≤ ∫⁻_A ofReal(ρ)·(‖(g(u) : ℝ)‖ₑ·ofReal(JF(u))) du = ofReal(ρ)·∫⁻_A ‖(g(u) : ℝ)‖ₑ·ofReal(JF(u)) du.
   The equality pulls out the finite constant ofReal(ρ) ≠ ∞ (lintegral_const_mul').
6. Steps 2 and 5 give the claim.
   If A = ∅, both sides are 0. The argument needs ρ ≥ 0 only at points u ∈ A, where it follows from ‖F(u)‖ ≤ ρ. ∎

    fun a b => continuous_inner.measurable.comp ((measurable_fderiv_apply_const ℝ G (EuclideanSpace.single a 1)).prodMk (measurable_fderiv_apply_const ℝ G (EuclideanSpace.single b 1)))
  have hdet : Measurable (fun z => Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun a b : Fin (k + 1) => inner ℝ (fderiv ℝ G z (EuclideanSpace.single a 1)) (fderiv ℝ G z (EuclideanSpace.single b 1)))) := by
    simp only [Matrix.det_apply]
    refine Finset.measurable_sum _ (fun σ _ => ?_)
    refine Measurable.const_smul ?_ _

proof_key_steps: f(z) = |g(τz)|·JG(z) is measurable: fderiv is Borel and the Gram determinant is a polynomial in the entries.
Tonelli on the cylinder (cylinder_fubini (b)) gives ∫⁻_{Cyl A} f = ∫⁻_A ∫⁻_{(0,1)} f(ι(t,u)) dt du.
For u ∈ A and t ∈ (0,1), gram_cone gives JG(ι(t,u)) = J(F u, t∂F u) = t^k J(F u, ∂F u) ≤ t^k‖F u‖JF(u) ≤ ρ·JF(u).
Integrate the pointwise bound over (0,1), which has measure 1, and then over A, pulling out the constant ofReal ρ.

audit.reason: The contract correctly requires neither Lipschitzness of G nor global positivity of ρ. Measurability of fderiv supplies the Tonelli integrand. The derivative tuple and gram_cone yield the pointwise estimate; integrating over the unit interval and extracting the finite ENNReal constant proves the exact bound. Nonnegativity of ρ follows at points of A, while the empty-set case is harmless. Both dependencies are correctly directed.
